Great question — this is a convention that trips up many genealogists reading Quaker records. Here's the history:

---

## Why Quakers Used Numbered Months

### The Core Religious Reason: Pagan Names Are Idolatrous

When George Fox founded the Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) in England in the 1640s–1650s, he and early Friends took seriously the biblical injunction not to honor false gods. The traditional month and day names were — and still are — rooted in paganism and Roman religion:

| Name | Origin |
|---|---|
| **January** | *Janus*, Roman god of doorways |
| **February** | *Februa*, Roman purification festival |
| **March** | *Mars*, Roman god of war |
| **April** | Possibly *Aphrodite* / Etruscan goddess Apru |
| **May** | *Maia*, Roman goddess |
| **June** | *Juno*, Roman goddess |
| **July** | Julius Caesar (deified emperor) |
| **August** | Augustus Caesar (deified emperor) |

The days of the week were equally problematic:
- **Sunday** → the Sun (worshipped)
- **Monday** → the Moon
- **Tuesday** → *Tiw*, Norse god
- **Wednesday** → *Woden*, Norse god
- **Thursday** → *Thor*, Norse god
- **Friday** → *Frigg*, Norse goddess
- **Saturday** → *Saturn*, Roman god

To speak these names was, to early Quakers, a subtle endorsement of idol worship. So they systematically replaced them: **First Month, Second Month … Twelfth Month** and **First Day, Second Day … Seventh Day.**

---

### The "Plain Speech" Movement

This was part of the broader Quaker testimony of *plainness* — rejecting the affectations and corruptions of the world. Just as Quakers used "thee" and "thou" to everyone equally (refusing to use "you" as a mark of social deference to elites), they used plain calendar language to refuse deference to false gods.

---

## The Critical Trap for Genealogists: Old Style vs. New Style Year

Here's where it gets complicated for researchers:

Before England adopted the Gregorian calendar in **1752**, the legal/civil year began on **25 March** (Lady Day), not 1 January. So in Quaker records:

- **"1st Month"** = **March** (because March was the first month of the year)
- **"2nd Month"** = April
- **"3rd Month"** = May
- …
- **"10th Month"** = December
- **"11th Month"** = January
- **"12th Month"** = February

After **1752**, when England switched to the Gregorian calendar and moved New Year's Day to 1 January, Quaker meeting records gradually shifted so that:

- **"1st Month"** = **January**
- **"2nd Month"** = February
- …and so on through the modern scheme.

This transition wasn't instantaneous — some meetings shifted earlier, some later — so **you must check the date of the record** to know which system applies.

---

## Practical Example

A Quaker birth record reading **"the 14th day of the 8th Month 1701"** means:

- **Pre-1752 reckoning**: 8th Month = October → **14 October 1701**
- **Post-1752 reckoning**: 8th Month = August → **14 August** (irrelevant here since it's 1701)

For this 1701 record, the answer is **14 October 1701** (Old Style).

---

## Why This Matters for Your Research

- **Dates can be misread by 2 months** if you don't account for the pre/post-1752 shift
- Quaker registers are among the most meticulous colonial-era American and English records — they recorded births, marriages, and deaths with great care — so getting the month right is essential
- Some transcription indexes have silently "corrected" numbered months incorrectly, introducing errors

If you need to convert a specific Quaker date, the `/convert-dates` skill can walk through the arithmetic precisely.

Sweden spent twelve years on a calendar shared by no other country. In 1699 they planned to migrate to the Gregorian calendar by simply skipping all leap days for 40 years (1700–1740). ## What "1750/1" normally means

In England before the Calendar Act took effect (1 Jan 1752), the legal year began on **25 March (Lady Day)**, not 1 January. Clerks therefore double-dated any event falling between **1 January and 24 March** to make clear which year they meant:

> "6 February 1750/1" → 1750 Old Style (OS) / **1751 New Style (NS)**

The rule is simple: for those dates, always use the **later** year (1751) in modern research notes.

---

## Why **25 March** 1750/1 is anomalous

The tool returned an error — not a conversion — because **25 March is the year-start day itself**:

> *"On March 25 the Old-Style year increments, so the Old-Style and New-Style years agree from that date onward. A slash written outside the window is anomalous."*

In other words, 25 March is the boundary. Everything **before** it (Jan 1–Mar 24) needs a double date. Everything **from** 25 March onward is already unambiguously in the new OS year — both calendars agree. A slash on 25 March itself is contradictory, and the tool explicitly declines to resolve it automatically.

---

## What to do in practice

1. **Check the surrounding register entries.** Look at the entries immediately before and after this marriage — do they seem to treat 25 March as the last day of 1750 or the first day of 1751? That local usage will tell you which year the clerk intended.

2. **Most likely explanation:** The clerk wrote "1750/1" by habit, using the double-date convention one day too late — in which case the intended year is **1751** (the new OS year beginning that very day). But do not silently resolve it; note the ambiguity.

3. **How to cite it in your research notes:**

   | What the record says | Recommended research-note form |
   |---|---|
   | 25 March 1750/1 | 25 March 1751 [OS; double date on year-start day — see note] |

   Add a brief source note explaining the anomaly so a future reader knows why you chose 1751.

---

**Bottom line:** Do not simply drop in "1751" without flagging it. Check the register's surrounding entries, note the scribal quirk, and record your reasoning. For every *other* double-dated English entry from 1 January through 24 March, the rule is straightforward: use the later year.
